newsitem.title: UK: UK's Labour opens last conference before election.
newsitem.headline: UK's Labour opens last conference before election.

text.p: Tony Blair's Labour party on Monday opened its last annual conference before an election, hoping for a trouble-free week to cement its huge poll lead and catapult it back to power after 17 years in opposition.

After defusing a row over pensions policy that threatened a showdown with left-wing traditionalists, the Labour leadership immediately set about wooing floating voters with an eye- catching pledge to end waiting lists for cancer surgery.

Health spokesman Chris Smith said the promise, to be paid for by slashing red tape in the health service, was a concrete example of how Labour would make a difference if it defeated the Conservatives at the next general election, which must be held no later than May.

Pledging to halt the encroaching privatisation of Britain's state-run health care system, Smith said: "Ask me why you should vote Labour. That reason will do alone. You will have a National Health Service again."

The pledge to redirect 100 million pounds ($156 million) a year from health service running costs to patient care is one of only a handful of specific, costed policies that Blair and his finance supremo, Gordon Brown, have been willing to make.

Labour is haunted by its candour at the last general election in 1992 when the Conservatives seized on its spending pledges to portray it as a party of crazed tax-raisers. Voters decided to play safe and re-elected Prime Minister John Major.

Determined not to offer similar openings at the next election, the Labour leadership on Sunday headed off a call for a three billion pound increase in basic pensions by referring the issue to a policy commission.
A former Labour cabinet minister, Baroness Barbara Castle, expressed dismay at the fudge. But Labour leaders, with a steely eye on the main prize of power, were unrepentant.
In his keynote speech to the conference later on Monday, Brown was expected to warn delegates of the need for "iron discipline" when choosing among public spending priorities.

Labour left-wingers, frustrated by nearly two decades in the political wilderness, have a long spending wish list and still openly chafe at what they see as the excessive caution of their new, moderate leaders.

"Because there's so much riding on winning the election, a lot of people are just grinning and bearing this and saying 'we've got to get in (to power), we won't make great rows at this conference'," Ken Livingstone, a leading left-winger, told BBC television.
But Brown is expected to give no ground to his critics, arguing that only by abandoning its old tax-and-spend policies can Labour fulfil its political goal of greater social justice.
"Our prudence is not the abandonment of socialism, but the essence of it," he will say, according to aides.

At the same stage before the 1992 election, the Conservatives held a two percentage point opinion poll lead over Labour. Today they are more than 20 points behind -- a gap that political analysts say is probably too large to close.

But Blair will have looked nervously at a Gallup poll in Monday's Daily Telegraph newspaper showing that Labour's margin had shrunk to 27 percentage points from 33. Individual polls have shown large differences in the size of Labour's lead.

Significantly, the survey revealed voters consider Labour -- following rows over Scottish policy and links to trade unions -- to be more divided that at any time since Blair became leader in July 1994.
